Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
Both hepatic lesions are small (2.2 cm in segment II and 3 cm in segment V) and are amenable to non‑major, segmental resections. Resection would preserve more than 70 % of functional liver parenchyma, maintain inflow/outflow of the remaining segments, and leave at least two contiguous segments (e.g., segments III‑IV‑VI‑VII‑VIII). No extra‑hepatic disease is present. Therefore an R0 liver resection is technically feasible without the need for portal vein embolisation or staged procedures.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Urgent control of the symptomatic primary tumor: perform a left‑sided colectomy (segmental or left hemicolectomy) to relieve the sub‑occlusive syndrome.  
• Because the liver resections are minor (segment II and segment V) and the colorectal operation is of moderate complexity, a simultaneous approach is reasonable in a fit 64‑year‑old patient with no comorbidities. Thus plan a combined left colectomy + segmental liver resections in the same operative session, provided intra‑operative assessment confirms adequate FLR and no unexpected findings.  
• If intra‑operative factors (excessive blood loss, hemodynamic instability, or unexpected liver disease) preclude a safe combined operation, defer liver resection and stage it 4–6 weeks after the colectomy, after recovery and repeat imaging to confirm unchanged hepatic disease.  
• Post‑operative systemic therapy: given RAS‑wild‑type status and high pre‑operative CEA, administer 6 months of adjuvant FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) as per current ESMO/ASCO guidelines for resected synchronous CRLM.  
• Surveillance: CEA and contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
The case provides the essential information (tumor size, location, number of liver metastases, RAS status, absence of extra‑hepatic disease, and patient fitness). No additional data are required to make a reliable resectability judgment or to formulate the surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases (segments II and V, 2.2 cm and 3 cm), bilobar but peripheral, without radiologic evidence of extrahepatic disease. Both lesions appear technically amenable to limited parenchymal-sparing resections (wedge/segmentectomy) with preservation of adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and favorable location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: management of the symptomatic primary tumor
• The subocclusive presentation makes the left colonic lesion the immediate priority.
• Perform an oncologic left colectomy first (or ileostomy) with lymphadenectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) to treat the obstruction risk and allow safe continuation of the oncologic strategy.
• Alternative : consider a temporary diversion before colectomy according to exact degree of subocclusion.

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery from colectomy
• After the emergent procedure, perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise 
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), the situation suggests biologically active disease; short-course neoadjuvant therapy allows treatment of micrometastases and assessment of tumor biology.
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT decision and tolerance.

C. Liver surgery after restaging (liver-first not indicated here due to symptoms)
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and CT restaging.
• If stability or response is observed, proceed to parenchymal-sparing liver resections: segment II wedge/segmentectomy and segment V wedge/segmentectomy guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 margins (>1mm) while preserving maximal liver parenchyma.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Post-hepatectomy therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including pre-operative cycles).
• Close postoperative surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially high tumor marker level.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact degree of subocclusion and whether an temporary diversion is required before colectomy.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of both metastases to confirm feasibility of parenchymal-sparing resections.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Exact location of the left colon tumor (descending vs sigmoid) influencing surgical planning.
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
G. Perform liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – The patient has a solitary 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, which can be removed with a limited hepatic resection (segmentectomy or wedge) while preserving > 30 % functional liver remnant. No extra‑hepatic disease is seen on PET, and the primary right‑colon lesion is amenable to standard right hemicolectomy. No anatomic or functional contraindications are present, therefore curative‑intent surgery can be performed immediately.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Pre‑operative work‑up  
   – Complete blood count, liver function tests, coagulation profile, and cardiopulmonary assessment (ASA, ECOG).  
   – Colonoscopy with biopsy (already done) to stage the primary (T/N) and obtain pathology.  
   – High‑resolution liver MRI or contrast‑enhanced CT with intra‑operative ultrasound planning to confirm solitary disease and exclude occult lesions.  

• Surgical plan (simultaneous resection)  
   1. Right hemicolectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy for the ileocecal primary.  
   2. Segment VI anatomical resection (or non‑anatomic wedge) aiming for R0 margin (≥1 mm).  
   3. Intra‑operative ultrasound to verify no additional hepatic lesions.  
   4. Ensure preservation of at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  

• Post‑operative oncologic management  
   – Pathology will define the stage of the colon cancer; assuming stage III or high‑risk stage II, initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab; anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective because of KRAS mutation).  
   – If the pathology shows node‑negative stage II disease, discuss the benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy versus observation, but most MDTs still offer 6 months of FOLFOX in the presence of a liver metastasis.  
   – Resume surveillance: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

• Rationale from literature  
   – Solitary colorectal liver metastasis is the classic indication for curative surgery (excerpt 1).  
   – Simultaneous resection is safe when the hepatic component is minor and the primary tumor is right‑sided without obstruction (excerpt discussing simultaneous vs staged approaches).  
   – KRAS mutation does not preclude surgery; it only influences choice of targeted agents (excerpt on molecular profile).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
No essential information is lacking for a reliable resectability assessment or surgical plan. The only data that would further refine adjuvant therapy decisions are:  
• Exact T and N stage of the primary tumor (pathology).  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidity profile.  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin).  
These items are routinely obtained before surgery and do not change the current recommendation.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
These items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the liver lesion (1.8 cm in segment III) is technically amenable to curative resection with adequate future liver remnant, and the upper‑rectal T3N1 primary is resectable by low‑anterior resection. However, definitive surgery cannot be performed immediately because short‑course pre‑operative radiotherapy (or chemoradiotherapy) for the rectal tumor is required before the colorectal resection. Completion of this radiotherapy is a prerequisite to proceeding with a curative‑intent combined operation.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Short‑course radiotherapy to the rectum (5 × 5 Gy) delivered now.  
• Restaging 4–6 weeks after radiotherapy with contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and pelvic MRI to confirm stability of the liver metastasis and adequacy of the primary‑tumor response.  
• If restaging confirms no new lesions and adequate liver remnant, proceed to a simultaneous minimally invasive operation:  
   – Laparoscopic low‑anterior resection of the upper rectal cancer with a protective loop ileostomy (optional based on intra‑operative assessment).  
   – Laparoscopic or open segment III non‑anatomic resection (or wedge resection) achieving R0 margins, preserving at least two contiguous liver segments and >30 % future liver remnant.  
• Post‑operative pathology review; if R0 resection of both sites is achieved, initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX) given N1 disease and elevated pre‑operative CEA.  
• Consider adding anti‑EGFR therapy (cetuximab) only if future disease progression occurs, as the tumor is RAS wild‑type.  
• Surveillance schedule: CEA every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months; contrast‑enhanced CT chest/abdomen and pelvic MRI at 6 months, then annually for at least 5 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Baseline liver function tests and calculation of future liver remnant volume (CT volumetry).  
• Cardiopulmonary fitness assessment (e.g., VO₂ max, echocardiogram) and ASA classification to confirm operative tolerance.  
• Detailed pelvic MRI report (distance of tumor from mesorectal fascia, sphincter involvement) to confirm feasibility of low‑anterior resection without need for abdominoperineal resection.  
• Full staging CT of chest to exclude occult pulmonary metastases.  
• Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity burden (Charlson index).  
These data are essential to finalize operative planning and confirm that simultaneous resection is safe.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
B. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT . Chest CT.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Detailed relationship of the liver lesion to segment III vascular structures on liver MRI.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – The three liver lesions are ≤3 cm, limited in number, and show only partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion, allowing an R0 resection with negative margins. No extra‑hepatic disease has been reported, and the MDT already considers the metastases “simple liver surgery possible,” implying that an adequate future liver remnant can be preserved. KRAS mutation and a high CEA are adverse prognostic markers but do not preclude curative resection. Therefore, from a technical and oncologic standpoint the disease meets criteria for immediate surgical resection.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Confirm complete staging before any operation:  
   – Contrast‑enhanced chest CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   – Full liver function panel, coagulation profile, and calculation of future liver remnant (CT volumetry or MRI).  
   – Assessment of performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and comorbidities (ASA, cardiac/pulmonary evaluation).  
• If the patient is medically fit (ECOG 0‑1, ASA ≤ 2, adequate FLR ≥ 30 % without prior chemotherapy or ≥ 40 % if pre‑treated):  
   – Proceed with a simultaneous curative approach:  
        – Standard oncologic resection of the transverse colon primary (right hemicolectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy, aiming for ≥ 1 mm circumferential margin).  
        – Limited hepatic resection – segmentectomy of segment IV and non‑anatomic wedge resections of segments V and VI, preserving at least two contiguous liver segments and ensuring negative margins.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to verify lesion boundaries and portal anatomy.  
   – No need for portal vein embolisation given the small volume to be removed.  
• If simultaneous surgery is deemed too demanding (e.g., borderline cardiopulmonary reserve, anticipated prolonged operative time):  
   – Stage the procedures: first resect the asymptomatic colon primary, allow recovery (≈ 4‑6 weeks), then perform hepatic resection.  
   – Alternatively, a liver‑first approach can be chosen if the primary is truly asymptomatic and the liver disease is at risk of progression; this also provides early pathological confirmation of response to any neoadjuvant therapy.  
• Peri‑operative systemic therapy:  
   – Because the disease is resectable and the patient has a KRAS‑mutated tumor, give 3 months of neoadjuvant oxaliplatin‑based doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX) ± bevacizumab before surgery only if the MDT wishes a “test of time” to confirm biologic stability (high CEA may support this).  
   – If upfront surgery is performed, plan adjuvant chemotherapy for 6 months (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) after recovery, as recommended for stage IV CRC with resected liver metastases.  
   – No anti‑EGFR agents are indicated due to KRAS mutation.  
• Post‑operative surveillance:  
   – CEA measurement every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   – Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest CT at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG) and ASA classification.  
• Detailed comorbidity profile (cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal function).  
• Baseline liver function tests and quantitative future liver remnant volume.  
• Full staging of the primary tumor (T‑stage, N‑stage) and any nodal involvement.  
• Confirmation that there is no extra‑hepatic disease (chest imaging, PET‑CT if available).  
• Patient’s preferences regarding simultaneous versus staged surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed vascular mapping on MRI to confirm absence of true portal invasion.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation in case of right hepatectomy.F. Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
Reasoning: • Four peripheral metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) each ≤ 3 cm are amenable to non‑anatomic wedge or segmental resections. • No involvement of major hepatic veins, portal/hepatic arteries, or biliary structures. • Resection can preserve at least two contiguous liver segments (e.g., left lateral sector and right posterior sector) leaving a future liver remnant well above the 30 % functional threshold for a patient with normal liver. • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on staging CT. All oncologic and technical criteria for an R0 resection are satisfied, therefore surgery can be performed without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   – Full liver function panel, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan to confirm adequate functional reserve.  
   – Volumetric CT or MRI to quantify future liver remnant (target ≥ 30 % of total liver volume).  
   – Cardiopulmonary assessment (ASA, ECOG) and optimization of comorbidities.  

2. Surgical plan (simultaneous resection)  
   – Primary tumor: sigmoid colectomy (low anterior resection or segmental resection) with adequate lymphadenectomy (aim ≥ 12 nodes).  
   – Liver: four peripheral metastases resected with wedge or segmental resections aiming for ≥ 1 mm margin (R0). No need for major hepatectomy; intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion number and location.  

3. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   – Start adjuvant FOLFOX (oxaliplatin‑based) within 6–8 weeks after surgery for 6 months; consider adding anti‑EGFR (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type and high pre‑operative CEA, especially if pathological risk factors (N1, synchronous disease) are present.  
   – Monitor CEA every 3 months and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years.  

4. Alternative staged approach (if intra‑operative assessment suggests liver resection will be more extensive than anticipated)  
   – Perform sigmoid resection first, allow 4–6 weeks recovery, then proceed with liver metastasectomy. Follow the same adjuvant chemotherapy schedule.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
No essential information is lacking for a reliable resectability judgment or management plan. The only optional data that could refine peri‑operative risk assessment are: • Quantitative future liver remnant volume measurement • Formal liver functional test (ICG‑R15 or mebrofenin scan) • Detailed cardiopulmonary fitness scores (e.g., VO₂ max). These are useful for safety confirmation but are not decisive for the resectability classification.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of each lesion.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
The two liver metastases (3 cm in segment II and 4 cm in segment IVa) are confined to the left liver, the middle hepatic vein is preserved, and the remaining right liver will constitute a future liver remnant well above the 30 %–35 % threshold. No extra‑hepatic disease has been reported, and imaging confirms that an R0 resection of both lesions is technically feasible while preserving inflow, outflow and biliary drainage. Therefore, from both technical and oncological standpoints the hepatic disease meets criteria for immediate resection without prerequisite down‑staging.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Baseline systemic staging – contrast‑enhanced chest CT (or PET‑CT) and full laboratory panel (including liver function, bilirubin, INR, platelets) to confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease and assess hepatic reserve.  
2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy – because the primary tumour is T4 N2 (high‑risk) and KRAS‑mutated, give 2–3 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab. This serves to (a) treat micrometastatic disease, (b) provide a biological test of tumour behaviour, and (c) may modestly improve disease‑free survival as supported by the literature.  
3. Restaging after chemotherapy – repeat multiphase CT/MRI of the liver and chest imaging. If the liver lesions are stable or responding and no new lesions appear, proceed to surgery. Progression would trigger a change to second‑line systemic therapy and reassessment of resectability.  
4. Surgical plan (simultaneous resection) –  
   • Right hemicolectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy (primary tumour control).  
   • Left hepatectomy encompassing segment II and segment IVa (or left lateral sectionectomy + segment IVa wedge) to achieve R0 margins; preserve the middle hepatic vein and ensure a right‑liver FLR > 30 % (≈ 55 % of total liver volume).  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude occult disease.  
   • If the patient’s cardiopulmonary reserve is marginal, consider a staged “liver‑first” approach (left hepatectomy first, followed by colectomy after recovery).  
5. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy – resume the same systemic regimen (FOLFOX + bevacizumab) to complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy, as recommended for high‑risk stage III colon cancer with synchronous liver metastases.  
6. Surveillance – CEA measurement and contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the abdomen every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually; chest imaging annually.

Step 3 – Missing data  
A reliable recommendation assumes that the following essential information is available:  

- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and cardiopulmonary reserve (ejection fraction, pulmonary function tests).

Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – The three liver metastases are small (1‑2 cm), limited in number, and confined to segments VI‑VIII of the right liver. Resection of these lesions can be achieved with non‑anatomic wedge resections or a limited segmentectomy, preserving a left‑liver future liver remnant well above the 30 % threshold. No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on PET, and the primary rectal tumor is T3N0, amenable to standard low anterior resection after short‑course radiotherapy. No oncologic or anatomic barrier mandates pre‑operative chemotherapy or further staging, therefore surgery can be planned without prior down‑staging.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) delivered now, as already planned.  
• Within 7‑10 days after radiotherapy, perform a simultaneous operation:  
   – Low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision (TME) and a protective diverting loop ileostomy if indicated.  
   – Liver‑first approach is not required; proceed with a limited right‑posterior hepatectomy (wedge resections of segments VI‑VIII) or a segmental resection, ensuring R0 margins and preserving ≥30 % FLR. Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to confirm lesion number and location.  
• Post‑operative care:  
   – Early recovery pathway, monitor liver function, and assess for any postoperative complications.  
   – After recovery (typically 4‑6 weeks), initiate adjuvant systemic therapy: 6 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given the RAS‑wild‑type status, to treat micrometastatic disease and reduce recurrence risk.  
   – Continue surveillance with serial CEA, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) and colonoscopy per standard guidelines.  
   – If pathology shows a complete response of the rectal primary (ypT0), discuss the possibility of a non‑operative “watch‑and‑wait” approach, but given the initial T3 stage, definitive surgical resection is preferred.

• Pre‑operative pelvic MRI to define circumferential resection margin (CRM) and assess mesorectal involvement.  
• Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidity profile to confirm fitness for combined surgery.

• Patient’s preference regarding stoma creation and postoperative quality‑of‑life considerations.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of hypertension, discovery of left colon cancer and a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 40 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, anatomically favorable for a single resection.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – The patient has a solitary 2.7 cm metastasis confined to segment IVb, no radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease, and a left‑sided primary. A limited hepatic resection (segment IVb wedge or left‑lateral sectionectomy) can achieve R0 margins while preserving >30 % future liver remnant. Age 70 and controlled hypertension do not preclude major surgery provided standard pre‑operative fitness assessment is satisfactory.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Pre‑operative work‑up  
  – Complete staging with contrast‑enhanced chest CT (or PET‑CT) and liver MRI to confirm absence of extra‑hepatic lesions and to delineate the hepatic lesion precisely.  
  – Baseline labs: liver function tests, bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance (if available), and assessment of cardiac/pulmonary reserve (ECOG 0‑1, ASA II‑III acceptable).  
  – Optimize hypertension and any other comorbidities.  

• Surgical plan (simultaneous resection)  
  – Perform oncologic resection of the left‑colon primary (segmental colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
  – Perform a parenchymal‑sparing hepatic resection of segment IVb (wedge resection or left‑lateral sectionectomy) aiming for ≥5 mm negative margin. Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude occult disease.  
  – Ensure preservation of at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage; anticipated FLR >30 % (or >0.5 % liver‑body‑weight ratio).  

• Post‑operative systemic therapy  
  – Given BRAF‑wild type, MSS status and a solitary metastasis, adjuvant chemotherapy is recommended to eradicate micrometastatic disease. Preferred regimen: 6 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) ± bevacizumab (if no contraindication).  
  – Consider enrollment in a clinical trial if available.  

• Surveillance  
  – CEA measurement every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
  – Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest CT at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
A definitive recommendation assumes that the following information is acceptable or will be confirmed:  
– ECOG performance status (or equivalent functional assessment).  
– Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance) to verify hepatic reserve.  
– Cardiopulmonary evaluation (e.g., echocardiogram, pulmonary function) to ensure tolerance of combined abdominal surgery.  
If any of these data are unavailable or reveal significant impairment, the plan would need to be adjusted (e.g., staged resection, portal vein embolization, or neoadjuvant chemotherapy).

The lesion is anatomically favorable for a a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm the relationship of the lesion to segment IVb vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology, however the KRAS status is unknown.

• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT.

B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)

Resectable upfront – The two liver metastases are small (2.1 cm and 2.4 cm), contiguous within segment VI, and can be removed by a limited anatomical segmentectomy while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments and an adequate future liver remnant (>30 %).    – Sigmoid colectomy with adequate proximal and distal margins and lymphadenectomy (T3N1).

   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to verify no additional occult lesions.  
• Post‑operative pathology review to confirm R0 margins, nodal status, and KRAS‑mutated status.  
• Adjuvant systemic therapy: given high CEA (180 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation (poor prognostic markers), administer 6 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) after recovery from surgery. Anti‑EGFR agents are contraindicated due to KRAS mutation.  
• Surveillance schedule: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the abdomen and chest CT annually (or sooner if CEA rises).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
No essential information is lacking to make a reliable resection and treatment plan. The case already provides tumor stage, metastatic burden, molecular status, and imaging that support an upfront simultaneous resection.

MDT Discussion: Deep but resectable metastasis, discussion of simultaneous versus sequential surgery.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- The patient has a solitary 3 cm metastasis confined to segment VII, which can be removed with a non‑anatomical or segmental resection while preserving >30 % functional liver remnant.  
- The primary tumour is located in the right colon and is amenable to a standard right hemicolectomy.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease, major comorbidities, or liver dysfunction are reported that would preclude curative surgery.  
- Therefore, both the colorectal primary and the hepatic lesion are technically resectable without the need for down‑staging or additional information.

   - Contrast‑enhanced chest CT to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   - Multiphasic liver MRI (or CT) to confirm solitary lesion, assess vascular anatomy and calculate future liver remnant (FLR).  
   - Baseline liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, albumin, and assessment of performance status (ASA, comorbidity index).  
2. Surgical plan (simultaneous resection)  
   - Perform a right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis.  
   - In the same operative session, perform a segment VII resection (or limited right posterior sectionectomy) aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm).  
   - Use low central venous pressure anesthesia to minimise hepatic bleeding.  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and exclude additional occult metastases.  
   - No need for portal vein embolisation given the small volume of liver to be removed.  
3. Post‑operative oncologic management  
   - Pathology review for T‑stage, N‑stage, grade, lymphovascular invasion, and margin status.  
   - Assuming R0 resection, initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX).  
   - Because the tumour is RAS wild‑type but right‑sided, add bevacizumab to the adjuvant regimen rather than anti‑EGFR therapy.  
   - Monitor CEA every 3 months and obtain surveillance imaging (CT chest/abdomen) at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years.  
4. Contingency  
   - If intra‑operative findings reveal additional liver lesions or inadequate FLR, convert to a staged approach (liver‑first or colon‑first) and consider pre‑operative chemotherapy to downsize disease.

- Detailed performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidity profile.  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and calculation of FLR volume.  
- Chest imaging results to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
- Exact T‑ and N‑stage of the primary tumour, histologic grade, presence of lymphovascular or perineural invasion.

- Patient’s preference regarding simultaneous versus staged surgery.

Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
Reasoning: The three liver metastases are confined to the left hepatic lobe, each ≤2.5 cm, and no extra‑hepatic disease is reported. Resection of the left lobe (segmental or left hepatectomy) would leave a substantial right‑lobe future liver remnant (>30 % of total liver volume) and satisfies the technical criteria of preserving two contiguous segments with adequate inflow, outflow and biliary drainage. There is no anatomic contraindication reported, and the primary sigmoid lesion is T3N0, amenable to curative resection. Therefore the disease is technically resectable without prerequisite interventions.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Baseline work‑up  
   – Full liver function panel, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan to confirm functional reserve.  
   – Volumetric CT or MRI to quantify future liver remnant (target ≥30 % in a normal liver).  
   – Performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and comorbidity assessment (cardiopulmonary evaluation).  
   – Staging PET‑CT or high‑resolution chest CT to reconfirm absence of occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

• Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (biological proof of disease biology)  
   – Because the metastases are synchronous, CEA is markedly elevated (150 ng/mL) and KRAS is mutated, initiate 3 months of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF).  
   – Re‑image with contrast‑enhanced MRI/CT after 2–3 cycles to assess response and ensure no progression.  

• Surgical plan (after confirming stable or responding disease)  
   – If the primary tumor is not obstructing or perforated, proceed with simultaneous resection: laparoscopic or open sigmoid colectomy with primary anastomosis plus left‑lateral segmentectomy/left hepatectomy aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm).  
   – If the primary tumor requires urgent management (obstruction, bleeding) or the patient’s operative risk is high, adopt a staged approach: (1) sigmoid resection first, recover 4–6 weeks, then liver resection; or (2) liver‑first if colorectal symptoms are minimal and liver disease is the dominant threat.  

• Intra‑operative adjuncts  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion number, size and relationship to vessels.  
   – Pringle maneuver as needed, but limit ischemia time (<15 min).  

• Post‑operative management  
   – Standard enhanced recovery pathway, monitor liver function, drain output.  
   – Resume systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOX‑bevacizumab) within 6–8 weeks for a total of 6 months peri‑operative chemotherapy (pre‑ + post‑operative).  
   – Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Quantitative future liver remnant volume (percentage or absolute volume).  
• Baseline liver function tests and any evidence of steatosis or fibrosis.  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (cardiovascular, pulmonary).  
• Detailed anatomic relationship of the three metastases to major hepatic vessels and biliary structures.  
• Confirmation that there is truly no extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., PET‑CT, chest CT).  
• Symptoms or complications of the primary sigmoid tumor (obstruction, bleeding, perforation).  
These data are needed to finalize the operative sequencing and to decide whether simultaneous resection is safe or a staged approach is preferable.

Woman, 66 years old, high rectal T3N1 cancer with a single 1.5 cm metastasis in segment II at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 50 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Peripheral resectable metastasis, possibility of combined surgery after pelvic treatment.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The solitary 1.5 cm metastasis in segment II meets technical criteria for hepatic resection (peripheral location, adequate future liver remnant, ability to achieve R0 margin). However, the rectal primary (high T3N1) requires neoadjuvant pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± chemotherapy) before definitive resection. Completion of this pre‑operative pelvic therapy is a prerequisite for any combined or simultaneous operation, thus the case is not resectable upfront.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Comprehensive restaging  
  • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) with liver‑specific contrast to confirm solitary lesion and assess FLR.  
  • High‑resolution pelvic MRI to define tumor height, mesorectal fascia involvement, and distance from sphincter.  
  • Chest CT to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
  • Baseline labs: liver function, bilirubin, ICG clearance or volumetry if concern for FLR.  
- Neoadjuvant pelvic therapy  
  • For a high rectal T3N1 lesion, either short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) followed by delayed surgery, or long‑course chemoradiation (45‑50 Gy with 5‑FU/Capecitabine) based on multidisciplinary consensus and patient factors.  
- Systemic chemotherapy during the interval  
  • Administer 3–4 cycles of a doublet (CAPOX or FOLFOX) ± biologic (anti‑EGFR such as cetuximab, given RAS‑wild type) to treat micrometastatic disease and potentially further shrink the liver lesion (although already small).  
- Restaging after neoadjuvant phase  
  • Repeat MRI pelvis and liver imaging, CEA measurement. Expect stable disease or response; confirm that the liver lesion remains resectable and no new extra‑hepatic disease has appeared.  
- Surgical sequencing  
  • Because the liver resection is minor (segment II non‑anatomic or segmentectomy) and the rectal resection is a low anterior resection, a simultaneous laparoscopic approach is feasible in a fit patient, offering reduced hospital stay and earlier systemic therapy completion.  
  • If intra‑operative concerns arise (e.g., limited FLR, extensive adhesions, or patient comorbidity), convert to a staged approach: first liver resection (segment II wedge/segmentectomy), followed by rectal surgery 6–8 weeks later after recovery.  
- Post‑operative management  
  • Complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (including the pre‑operative cycles).  
  • Consider adjuvant capecitabine‑oxaliplatin (CAPOX) if not already given, given node‑positive disease.  
  • Monitor CEA and imaging (CT chest/abdomen) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Performance status / ECOG score and detailed comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Baseline liver function tests and quantitative future liver remnant volume.  
- Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge and mesorectal fascia status on MRI.  
- Results of chest imaging to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
- Patient’s preference regarding simultaneous versus staged surgery.  
- Details of any prior abdominal surgeries that might affect operative planning.
Reference:

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left T4aN2 colon cancer, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Max size 3.8 cm. CEA 330 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Limited liver involvement, potentially curative upfront.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Three liver metastases (segments IV, V, VIII) each ≤ 3.8 cm; total tumor burden well below the 30 % future liver remnant threshold for a patient with normal liver.  
- Anatomically feasible to achieve R0 resection with non‑anatomic wedge resections or limited segmentectomies while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow, outflow and biliary drainage.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease reported on staging CT.  
- Imaging quality (triphasic CT) appears sufficient for surgical planning.  
Therefore the hepatic disease meets technical criteria for immediate resection; no prerequisite intervention or missing critical information is identified.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative systemic therapy (optional but recommended)  
   - Given high‑risk primary features (T4a, N2, KRAS‑mutated, CEA 330 ng/mL), administer 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) to assess tumor biology and treat micrometastatic disease.  
   - Restage with contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI after chemotherapy; confirm no progression of hepatic lesions and absence of new extra‑hepatic sites.  

2. Surgical sequencing  
   - If the primary tumor is asymptomatic and the patient has adequate physiologic reserve: proceed with a simultaneous operation – left‑sided colectomy (segmental resection with adequate mesocolic clearance) combined with hepatic resection of the three metastases.  
   - If the primary tumor is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or the patient’s operative risk is high: adopt a liver‑first approach – resect hepatic lesions first, then address the colon primary after recovery (typically 4–6 weeks later).  

3. Hepatic resection plan  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion number, size and location.  
   - Perform non‑anatomic wedge resections of segments IV, V and VIII or limited segmentectomies (e.g., segment IVb, segment V, segment VIII) aiming for ≥ 1 mm microscopic margin (R0).  
   - Preserve at least two contiguous segments (e.g., left lateral sector + right posterior sector) to ensure FLR > 30 % of total liver volume.  
   - No need for portal vein embolization or two‑stage hepatectomy given the modest volume loss.  

4. Post‑operative management  
   - Pathology review of primary and hepatic specimens; confirm R0 margins.  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (total of 6 months peri‑operative therapy) to address residual microscopic disease.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
All essential information for a reliable resectability and treatment plan is available: age, performance status (assumed adequate), primary tumor stage, nodal status, KRAS mutation, CEA level, number, size and distribution of liver metastases, and absence of extra‑hepatic disease on imaging. No additional data are required at this stage.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 3 lesions to segment IV, V et VIII vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.

• The very high CEA level (330 ng/mL), T4aN2 primary tumor, KRAS mutation and multiplicity of lesions indicate biologically aggressive disease.
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.

• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• After recovery, left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with anastomosis
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.

F. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles).

Because these decisive pieces of information are missing, the lesion set is considered “potentially resectable” pending confirmation of adequate FLR and patient fitness.

1. Baseline work‑up  
   - Obtain liver‑specific MRI with diffusion‑weighted and hepatobiliary contrast sequences for precise lesion mapping.  
   - Perform volumetric CT/MRI to calculate FLR.

   - Primary tumor is right‑sided colon cancer (right hemicolectomy) with no obstruction or perforation.

- Full molecular profile of the primary tumor (RAS mutation status, MSI/MMR).  
- Details on any prior systemic therapy (none reported, but confirmation needed).  

These data are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive “resectable upfront” decision and to tailor the optimal peri‑operative oncologic plan.

Man, 57 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven bilobar liver metastases, sizes 1 to 4 cm at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 520 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: vascular contact with the right portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Metastases not resectable upfront, considered for conversion chemotherapy FOLFOX + bevacizumab.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the case requires a prerequisite action before surgery: down‑staging with conversion systemic therapy (FOLFOX + bevacizumab) and subsequent reassessment of tumor burden, future liver remnant (FLR) volume and vascular involvement. Until an adequate FLR and clear margins can be achieved, upfront resection is not feasible.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate conversion chemotherapy: FOLFOX plus bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
- Schedule imaging reassessment (contrast‑enhanced CT or liver‑specific MRI) after 3–4 cycles (≈6–8 weeks) to evaluate:  
   • Size reduction of each metastasis, especially those abutting the right portal branch.  
   • Number of viable lesions remaining.  
   • Future liver remnant volume (target ≥ 30 % in a normal liver, ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected).  
- If response is adequate and FLR is sufficient:  
   • Plan curative‑intent liver surgery.  
   • Consider a liver‑first approach because the primary tumor is T4aN2 but not obstructed; this avoids delaying control of hepatic disease.  
   • Perform right‑sided colon resection (extended right hemicolectomy) either simultaneously (if operative time and patient fitness allow) or in a second staged operation after hepatic resection.  
   • Surgical technique: aim for R0 resection of all seven lesions; use intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate margins; for lesions touching the right portal branch, perform parenchymal‑sparing segmental resection or limited portal vein reconstruction if needed.  
- If FLR is insufficient after chemotherapy response:  
   • Proceed to portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branch to induce hypertrophy of the left liver, then re‑image after 3–4 weeks.  
   • If still inadequate, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage non‑anatomic resections or ablations of right‑lobe disease, followed by PVE and second‑stage left‑lobe resection).  
- For any residual small lesions (<1 cm) in difficult locations after the main resection, consider adjunctive local therapy (radiofrequency ablation or stereotactic body radiotherapy) to achieve complete clearance.  
- Post‑operative management:  
   • Pathology review of primary and liver specimens; confirm negative margins.  
   • Resume systemic chemotherapy (same regimen or switch to FOLFIRI if progression) for a total of 6 months adjuvant therapy, adjusted for postoperative recovery.  
   • Serial CEA monitoring and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and quantitative FLR calculation.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Detailed assessment for extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., chest CT/PET for lung mets, bone scan if indicated).  
- Exact anatomical relationship of the metastases to the right portal branch (degree of encasement, need for vascular reconstruction).  
- Whether the primary colon tumor is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) that would dictate priority of colon resection.  
- Planned duration and number of chemotherapy cycles before re‑evaluation.

   – Re‑image the liver (contrast‑enhanced MRI) to assess response of each lesion, especially the RHV‑contacting metastasis.  
   – Re‑calculate FLR; if FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % for chemotherapy‑injured liver) and all lesions can be cleared with negative margins, proceed to a single‑stage parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (segmental resections of II, III, VI, VIII with possible R1 vascular resection of RHV if needed).

5. Adjuvant therapy  
   – Complete peri‑operative chemotherapy to a total of 6 months (including pre‑operative cycles) and consider postoperative FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR for 3–4 cycles, guided by pathologic response and postoperative CEA trend.

Man, 63 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥8 lesions), maximum size 4.5 cm, partial contact with the IVC at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 890 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, potentially resectable after major response to FOLFOXIRI.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The liver disease is extensive (≥8 lesions, largest 4.5 cm) with partial IVC contact, making an R0 resection unlikely without tumor downsizing and/or augmentation of the future liver remnant (FLR).  
- The MDT explicitly states that resection may become feasible after a major response to FOLFOXIRI, indicating a prerequisite systemic‑therapy response.  
- No current data on FLR volume, liver function, or patient performance status are provided, both of which are essential to confirm technical feasibility.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Induction systemic therapy: Start FOLFOXIRI (folinic acid, 5‑FU, oxaliplatin, irinotecan) ± anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab) or anti‑EGFR (cetuximab) given the left‑sided, BRAF‑wild‑type tumor. Aim for 3–4 months (≈8–12 cycles) with radiologic assessment after every 2 months.  
- Response assessment: Perform contrast‑enhanced multiphase CT or liver‑specific MRI to evaluate:  
  • Reduction in number/size of lesions, especially those abutting the IVC.  
  • Preservation of vascular inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
  • Calculation of FLR (target ≥30 % in normal liver, ≥40 % if prior chemotherapy‑associated liver injury).  
- If adequate response and FLR:  
  • Plan a single‑stage curative hepatectomy (e.g., right posterior sectionectomy + wedge resections) combined with simultaneous or staged resection of the primary colon tumor, depending on symptomatology and operative risk.  
- If FLR insufficient after downsizing:  
  • Perform portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy, followed by a second‑stage resection once FLR reaches safe volume.  
- If response is suboptimal or disease progresses:  
  • Switch to second‑line systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) and reassess for possible conversion.  
  • Consider locoregional therapies (e.g., stereotactic body radiotherapy, radiofrequency ablation) for residual lesions not amenable to resection.  
- Primary tumor management:  
  • If the colon primary is asymptomatic after systemic therapy, a simultaneous colectomy (left‑sided resection) with liver surgery can be performed by an experienced colorectal‑hepatic team.  
  • If symptomatic or high risk of obstruction/bleeding, resect the primary first, then proceed with liver‑first approach after recovery.  
- Adjuvant phase: After complete (R0) liver and primary resection, give 6 months of postoperative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
- Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT/MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Current performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidity burden (Charlson index).  
- Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and assessment of chemotherapy‑induced liver injury.  
- Quantitative FLR volume (CT volumetry or MRI) and calculation of liver‑to‑body‑weight ratio.  
- Precise vascular anatomy: extent of IVC and hepatic vein involvement, need for vascular reconstruction.  
- Full staging for extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT/PET‑CT for lung, peritoneum, bone).  
- KRAS/NRAS mutation status and MSI/MMR status to guide biologic choice.  
- Patient’s preferences regarding aggressive multimodal therapy.

Case_Content:
Woman, 52 years old, T3N2 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with bilobar liver metastases (six lesions, 2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 600 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: invasion of the middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Not initially resectable, goal of volumetric reduction with chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Bilobar disease with six lesions (2–5 cm) and documented invasion of the middle hepatic vein makes an R0 resection impossible with the current anatomy.  
- The future liver remnant (FLR) is likely <30 % after a curative‑intent hepatectomy, especially if the middle hepatic vein must be sacrificed, violating the technical criterion of preserving at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, but the case lacks quantitative FLR volume, liver function tests, and performance status, all of which are decisive for immediate surgery.  
- Therefore, conversion to resectability will require (a) down‑staging systemic chemotherapy and (b) a hypertrophy‑inducing maneuver (portal vein embolisation / two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS) to obtain a sufficient FLR before any definitive liver resection.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy (step‑by‑step)  
1. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Start a 4–6 cycle oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) plus bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
   - Assess response after every two cycles with RECIST and CEA trend; aim for ≥30 % reduction in total tumor volume.  

2. Re‑assessment of hepatic burden (≈6–8 weeks after induction)  
   - Perform triphasic CT and liver‑specific MRI with volumetry.  
   - Calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % after chemotherapy‑induced liver injury), plan a hypertrophy strategy.  

3. Hypertrophy maneuver (if needed)  
   - Right (or left, depending on planned resection) portal vein embolisation (PVE) to induce FLR growth; reassess FLR 2–4 weeks later.  
   - If FLR remains insufficient or tumor involvement of the middle hepatic vein persists, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) or ALPPS, using intra‑operative ultrasound to guide parenchymal‑sparing resections and possible R1 vascular resection if margin <1 mm but vessel reconstruction is feasible.  

4. Liver‑first surgical phase (once adequate FLR achieved)  
   - Aim for parenchymal‑sparing resection: non‑anatomic wedge resections of peripheral lesions; preserve the middle hepatic vein if oncologically safe, otherwise resect with vascular reconstruction (R1‑vascular acceptable in KRAS‑mutated disease).  
   - Perform intra‑operative ultrasound and, if needed, adjunctive thermal ablation (MWA) for lesions ≤3 cm that are difficult to resect.  

5. Management of the rectal primary  
   - After hepatic surgery (or concurrently if patient fitness allows), deliver long‑course chemoradiotherapy for the T3N2 upper rectal cancer (45 Gy + 5‑FU‑based radiosensitiser).  
   - Re‑stage the rectum 6–8 weeks post‑CRT; proceed to definitive low‑anterior resection with total mesorectal excision (or abdominoperineal resection if sphincter involvement persists).  

6. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Complete peri‑operative chemotherapy to a total of 6 months (e.g., additional 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX after liver resection, then 3 cycles after rectal surgery).  
   - Continue bevacizumab only if the interval from the last dose exceeds 6 weeks before major surgery to reduce wound‑healing complications.  

7. Surveillance  
   - CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 3 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (percentage of total liver) and liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities that could affect major hepatectomy or chemoradiotherapy tolerance.  
- Detailed assessment of the extent of middle hepatic vein invasion (length of involvement, possibility of reconstruction).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung nodules) on high‑resolution chest CT or PET‑CT.  
- Molecular profile beyond KRAS (BRAF, MSI/dMMR) which may influence systemic therapy choices.  
- Baseline cardiopulmonary reserve to tolerate combined liver and rectal surgery.

Woman, 55 years old, left T3N2M1 colon cancer, seven liver metastases, some coalescent in the hilar region at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, maximum size 5.5 cm. CEA 800 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Borderline disease, possible two-stage hepatectomy after effective chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Seven bilobar metastases, largest 5.5 cm, with coalescent lesions near the hilum make a single‑stage curative resection technically infeasible while preserving ≥2 contiguous segments and an adequate future liver remnant (FLR).  
- Conversion to resectability requires (a) systemic chemotherapy to downsize disease and test tumor biology, and (b) FLR augmentation (portal vein embolisation or a staged hepatectomy) before definitive surgery.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Induction systemic therapy: Begin a KRAS‑mutated‑appropriate regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) for 2–3 months; monitor CEA and repeat high‑resolution liver MRI/CT after each 2‑cycle block.  
- Response assessment: If imaging shows ≥20 % reduction in total tumor volume or stable disease without new lesions, and FLR volumetry remains <30 % of total liver, proceed to FLR augmentation.  
- FLR augmentation: Perform right (or left) portal vein embolisation (or ligation) targeting the lobe that will be resected first, aiming for ≥30–35 % FLR hypertrophy within 4–6 weeks.  
- First‑stage hepatectomy: Resect the less‑diseased lobe (e.g., right hepatectomy if right‑dominant disease) together with any resectable lesions in that lobe; intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm clearance; preserve inflow/outflow of the future remnant.  
- Interval reassessment: Repeat imaging and CEA; confirm FLR growth and absence of disease progression.  
- Second‑stage hepatectomy: Complete resection of remaining lesions in the hypertrophied remnant (e.g., left hepatectomy or extended left lateral resection) aiming for R0 margins.  
- Primary colon tumor: If the primary is not obstructing, adopt a liver‑first approach; otherwise, perform a diverting colostomy or resect the primary before chemotherapy. After hepatic clearance, perform definitive left‑sided colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy.  
- Adjuvant therapy: Resume/continue systemic chemotherapy post‑hepatectomy (total 6 months of peri‑operative therapy) and consider postoperative targeted therapy per KRAS status.  
- Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT/MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and quantitative FLR volume.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity burden (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum) on chest CT/PET.  
- Details of primary tumor symptoms (obstruction, bleeding) and need for urgent colorectal surgery.  
- Exact anatomical distribution of each hepatic lesion (segmental map) to plan resection margins and PVE target.  
- Planned chemotherapy regimen and patient’s tolerance to intensive triplet therapy.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right T4aN2 colon cancer, ten bilobar liver metastases (1-4 cm) at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 1350 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type. Liver MRI: contact with IVC and left portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Not initially resectable, induction therapy planned before re-evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The MDT has already judged the disease “not initially resectable” because ten bilobar metastases (1‑4 cm) involve critical vascular structures (IVC, left portal branch) and the future liver remnant is uncertain. Conversion to resectability therefore requires a prerequisite action – systemic induction (neoadjuvant) chemotherapy to achieve tumor downsizing and to allow reassessment of technical feasibility. This meets the definition of “Potentially resectable” (requires prior action before surgery).

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive conversion chemotherapy: preferred regimen is a triplet (FOLFOXIRI) combined with a biologic agent (bevacizumab) given the high tumor burden and elevated CEA; adjust to doublet if toxicity concerns.  
- Re‑image after 2–3 months (contrast‑enhanced MRI with liver‑specific contrast) to assess tumor response, volumetric FLR, and vascular involvement.  
- If response is adequate (≥30 % reduction in sum of diameters, or sufficient shrinkage of lesions abutting IVC/portal branch) and FLR is <30 % of total liver volume, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the future remnant.  
- Re‑evaluate after PVE (2–4 weeks). If FLR reaches ≥30 % (or ≥0.5 % body weight) and all lesions are amenable to R0 resection, proceed with a liver‑first approach:  
   • Stage 1 – extended right hepatectomy or combined right hepatectomy + segmental left‑lobe resections, using intra‑operative ultrasound to achieve negative margins; consider adjunctive thermal ablation or stereotactic body radiotherapy for lesions inseparable from major vessels.  
   • Stage 2 (4–6 weeks later) – definitive resection of the primary right‑sided colon cancer (right hemicolectomy) after hepatic recovery, unless the primary is symptomatic and requires earlier surgery.  
- If conversion is insufficient or FLR remains inadequate despite PVE, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (right‑sided resection first, interval growth, then left‑sided completion) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) in a high‑volume center.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen or maintenance with fluoropyrimidine + anti‑VEGF) for at least 3 months, guided by pathology (margin status, nodal involvement).  
- Throughout, monitor CEA trends and consider PET‑CT if biochemical rise suggests occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidity burden (Charlson index).  
- Baseline liver function tests and indocyanine‑green clearance to predict postoperative hepatic reserve.  
- Precise volumetric measurement of future liver remnant (FLR) before and after any planned PVE.  
- Detailed anatomic map of each metastasis relative to hepatic veins, portal branches, and the IVC (segmental location).  
- Confirmation of KRAS/NRAS mutation status (in addition to BRAF wild‑type) to refine biologic risk and choice of targeted therapy.  
- Assessment for extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum) via chest CT or PET‑CT.  
- Patient’s willingness for aggressive multimodal therapy and anticipated postoperative quality of life.

• Two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections with or without combined tumor ablation guided by imaging depending on response pattern.

• Right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) should be coordinated according to response and patient condition (ideally after liver surgery).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.
