Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, left T4aN2M1 colon cancer with multiple bilobar metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + bevacizumab: 60% volumetric reduction, CEA dropped from 880 to 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: 5 remaining lesions, well-defined.
MDT Discussion: Major response to chemotherapy, surgical conversion considered.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Classification: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab the liver disease has shrunk by ~60 % and only five well‑defined lesions remain, which makes an R0 hepatic resection technically feasible in many centres.  
- However, critical information required to confirm that a safe, curative hepatectomy can be performed is missing: the calculated future liver remnant (FLR) volume, the exact size and segmental distribution of each lesion, their relationship to major vessels/ducts, and the current liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets).  
- Without these data we cannot guarantee that the FLR will be sufficient after resection or that portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage approach will be needed. Therefore the case falls into the “Potentially resectable” category, pending acquisition of the missing parameters.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy (step‑by‑step)  
- 1. Complete the current pre‑operative assessment: obtain high‑quality contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) with volumetric analysis, liver function tests, and a full extra‑hepatic work‑up (chest CT/PET‑CT).  
- 2. Multidisciplinary review of the imaging to define:  
   • FLR percentage (target ≥ 30 % for a normal liver, ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected).  
   • Feasibility of a parenchymal‑sparing, single‑stage hepatectomy versus a staged strategy (PVE‑assisted or two‑stage hepatectomy).  
- 3. If FLR is adequate (≥ 30‑35 % and liver function is normal):  
   • Plan a simultaneous or sequential resection. Because the primary tumour is left‑sided T4aN2, schedule a curative colectomy (e.g., extended left hemicolectomy) followed by liver resection in the same operation if operative risk is acceptable, or perform the colon resection first and the liver resection within 4‑6 weeks.  
   • Use intra‑operative ultrasound to guide parenchymal‑sparing resections of the five lesions, aiming for R0 margins (≥ 1 mm) and preserving at least two contiguous segments.  
- 4. If FLR is insufficient:  
   • Perform portal vein embolization (or liver venous deprivation) of the lobe to be resected, re‑image after 2‑4 weeks to confirm hypertrophy, then proceed with a single‑stage major hepatectomy or a classic two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage clears the future liver remnant, second stage completes resection after hypertrophy).  
- 5. Post‑operative systemic therapy:  
   • Resume FOLFOX ± bevacizumab for a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (completion of the planned 12 cycles, counting pre‑operative 6 cycles).  
   • Consider adjuvant oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy for the primary tumour (standard 6‑month FOLFOX) if not already incorporated.  
- 6. Surveillance:  
   • CEA and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 3‑4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data essential for a definitive plan  
- Quantitative FLR volume and percentage after planned resection.  
- Exact maximal diameter of each hepatic lesion and their segmental locations (relationship to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, biliary ducts).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, platelet count) and any evidence of chemotherapy‑induced liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants, distant nodes) on recent chest CT/PET‑CT.  
- Molecular profile of the tumour (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF status) to guide any further targeted therapy.  
- Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities that could affect operative risk.  
- Status of the primary colon tumour (already resected, pending resection, or symptomatic).  

Acquiring these data will allow conversion of the “Potentially resectable” classification to either “Resectable upfront” (if FLR is adequate) or “Not resectable” (if disease is still extensive or extra‑hepatic spread precludes cure).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab, the patient shows a major radiologic and biologic response (≈60% volumetric reduction; CEA from 880 to 180 ng/mL). MRI now demonstrates five well-defined residual liver lesions without reported extrahepatic disease. In this context of marked downsizing and clearer lesion delineation, a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant appears potentially achievable. This pattern is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Immediate high-quality restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to reassess precise segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships after tumor shrinkage and a chest CT scan.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical conversion strategy
• If imaging confirms feasibility, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of all five lesions guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may be performed as a single-stage or staged hepatectomy.
• The goal is complete clearance of residual disease while preserving maximal functional parenchyma.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic chemotherapy after recovery to complete a total of approximately 6 months of treatment (including preoperative cycles).

E. Surveillance
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially very high tumor burden.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of the five residual lesions on post-chemotherapy MRI and detailed vascular and biliary relationships after tumor shrinkage.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. chest CT scan
F. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, sigmoid tumor with eight bilobar liver metastases. After 4 months FOLFIRI: radiological stability, CEA unchanged at 420 ng/mL. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases.
MDT Discussion: Stable disease, not resectable, discussion on continuing systemic therapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has eight bilobar metastases, which exceeds the classic “up‑front” resectable threshold, but modern strategies (parenchymal‑sparing, two‑stage hepatectomy, portal‑vein embolisation, ALPPS) can convert many such cases. Critical information that determines whether conversion is feasible is missing – specifically the future liver remnant (FLR) volume, the size and exact anatomic relationship of each lesion to major vessels/biliary structures, and the quality of the non‑tumorous liver (steatosis, chemotherapy‑associated injury). Without these data we cannot declare the disease unresectable outright, but we must require further assessment and likely down‑staging before surgery.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Continue systemic therapy with a regimen that maximises tumour‑shrinkage potential:  
   – If not already combined with a biologic, add bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) to FOLFIRI, or switch to a more intensive doublet (FOLFOX) or triplet (FOLFOXIRI) based on tolerability and molecular profile.  
   – Obtain tumour molecular testing (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H) to decide on anti‑EGFR therapy if RAS wild‑type and left‑sided primary.  
• Re‑image the liver (contrast‑enhanced MRI with hepatobiliary contrast or high‑resolution CT) after 2–3 months of the intensified regimen; repeat CEA.  
• If imaging shows ≥ 30 % reduction in total tumour volume, or a decrease in number of lesions, proceed to a detailed surgical planning session:  
   – Calculate FLR; if FLR < 20‑30 % (depending on liver quality), schedule portal‑vein embolisation (PVE) or consider ALPPS to induce hypertrophy.  
   – Plan a parenchymal‑sparing, staged hepatectomy (e.g., right‑plus‑left lateral resection in two operations) or a combined resection/ablation approach for lesions abutting critical structures.  
   – Ensure R0 margins (> 1 mm) can be achieved while preserving at least two contiguous functional liver segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
• If disease remains stable but FLR is adequate, a two‑stage hepatectomy or simultaneous resection (if patient fitness permits) can be contemplated.  
• If progression occurs (new lesions, growth of existing lesions, rising CEA), continue systemic therapy; consider enrollment in a clinical trial or shift to best‑supportive care if performance status declines.  
• Throughout, maintain surveillance of the primary sigmoid tumour; if not yet resected and symptomatic, schedule colorectal resection either before or after hepatic surgery according to a liver‑first or simultaneous approach, guided by symptom burden and patient fitness.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile.  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and assessment of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
• Precise volumetric measurement of future liver remnant.  
• Detailed size, location, and vascular/biliary involvement of each of the eight metastases.  
• Molecular profile of the tumour (KRAS/NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR).  
• Status of the primary sigmoid tumour (resected vs. pending, symptomatic).  
• Whether a biologic agent (bevacizumab, anti‑EGFR) has already been used with FOLFIRI.  
• Patient’s nutritional status and any pre‑existing liver disease (steatosis, fibrosis).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases and, after 4 months of FOLFIRI, shows radiological stability with persistently elevated CEA (420 ng/mL). The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and absence of meaningful tumor downsizing make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered potentially resectable after major conversion.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Continuation and adaptation of systemic therapy
• Given the absence of radiologic response and stable high CEA, modification of the systemic regimen should be considered according to MDT discussion.
• The objective remains to achieve tumor downsizing sufficient to allow potential secondary resectability.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to detect any delayed response or change in lesion distribution.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant reduction in lesion size and number occurs, enabling parenchymal-sparing resections or multiples ablations or staged hepatectomy with adequate future liver remnant.

D. Alternative local strategies
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of all eight lesions on MRI.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case of potential future resection.
C. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation.
D. Status of the primary sigmoid tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for ongoing systemic therapy.
F. Complete extrahepatic staging to confirm disease confinement to the liver.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Current imaging shows a partial response but the exact number, size, and segmental distribution of the remaining liver lesions are not provided.  
- No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, vascular or biliary involvement, or liver functional reserve.  
- Because these decisive pieces of information are missing, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” The prerequisite action is a detailed volumetric and anatomical reassessment (including FLR calculation and vascular mapping) after further systemic therapy to determine whether an R0 resection with adequate FLR is feasible.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI) for another 2–3 months, adding a biologic agent if molecular profile permits (anti‑EGFR for RAS‑wild‑type, anti‑VEGF otherwise).  
- Perform restaging with contrast‑enhanced MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) and triphasic CT of chest/abdomen to:  
  • Quantify residual liver lesions (size, number, segmental location).  
  • Assess relationship to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
  • Calculate FLR volume; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % with chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS.  
- Evaluate the primary rectal tumor: if asymptomatic, defer definitive rectal surgery until after hepatic clearance (liver‑first approach). If symptomatic (bleeding, obstruction), treat with short‑course radiotherapy and/or surgical resection before liver surgery.  
- Once imaging confirms that all viable metastases can be removed with negative margins while preserving ≥2 contiguous liver segments and an adequate FLR, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection:  
  • Aim for an R0 anatomical or non‑anatomical resection of each lesion; combine with intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult disease.  
  • For lesions in locations that would compromise FLR, consider adjunctive local therapies (RFA, SBRT) to achieve complete clearance.  
- Post‑operative management: resume adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 3–6 months of FOLFOXIRI ± targeted agent) and monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact number, size, and segmental location of residual liver metastases after chemotherapy.  
- Relationship of lesions to major hepatic vessels and biliary structures.  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume and liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count).  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities affecting surgical risk.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS/NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide targeted therapy.  
- Status of the primary rectal tumor (local stage, symptoms, response to any neoadjuvant radiotherapy).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Trend of tumor markers (CEA) after systemic therapy.  
- Tolerance and cumulative dose of prior chemotherapy (risk of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury).

A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.

• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
