   - If hepatic disease is controlled and FLR is adequate (or after successful PVE), proceed with hepatic resection first.  
   - Choose an anatomic or non‑anatomic resection strategy that achieves R0 margins while preserving ≥2 contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow.  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance; consider adjunctive thermal ablation for lesions in difficult locations.  

5. Rectal resection  
   - After hepatic surgery and a short recovery (4–6 weeks), perform total mesorectal excision (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection depending on residual tumor involvement) with a protective stoma as indicated.  
   - Pathology will guide need for further adjuvant therapy.  

6. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Continue pembrolizumab for at least 2 years or until disease progression, per MSI‑H guidelines.  
   - If residual high‑risk features are identified (e.g., positive nodes, close margins), consider adding adjuvant oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy.

- Detailed liver imaging: size of each metastasis, segmental distribution, proximity to hepatic veins/portal pedicles, and calculated future liver remnant volume.

  • Begin a HER2‑targeted doublet (e.g., trastuzumab + pertuzumab or trastuzumab + lapatinib/tucatinib) combined with a standard doublet chemotherapy backbone (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).

  • Liver‑first approach (preferred when the primary tumor is asymptomatic):

  • Consider maintenance HER2 blockade (e.g., trastuzumab alone) for up to 12 months, especially if residual microscopic disease is a concern.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, T3N1M1 upper rectal tumor, liver metastases (3-5 cm) with contact with IVC and right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 580 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Complex central metastases, discussion on combined approach or venous reconstruction.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The liver metastases are in close contact with the inferior vena cava and the right hepatic vein, indicating major vascular involvement that may require reconstruction.  
- No data are provided on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, the exact number and bilobar distribution of lesions, or the degree of encasement of the vessels.  
- Because a definitive decision on whether an R0 resection can be achieved while preserving adequate FLR and vascular inflow/outflow cannot be made, the case requires further evaluation (e.g., neoadjuvant chemotherapy to assess tumor biology and possible down‑staging, and volumetric imaging to calculate FLR).  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) as a conversion regimen; this serves to (a) treat micrometastatic disease, (b) assess tumor biology, and (c) potentially shrink the liver lesions away from the IVC/HV.  
- For the rectal primary, give short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) or long‑course chemoradiation if symptomatic or threatening the mesorectal fascia; a diverting stoma can be placed if obstruction is a concern.  
- Restage after 2–3 cycles of chemotherapy with high‑resolution liver MRI and triphasic CT; obtain volumetric analysis of FLR.  
- If FLR is <30 % of total liver volume, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) to induce hypertrophy; re‑image 2–3 weeks later to confirm adequate FLR.  
- Once adequate FLR and acceptable tumor‑vascular relationship are confirmed, proceed with a liver‑first (reverse) approach:  
   • Extended right hepatectomy (or right trisection) with en‑bloc resection of the right hepatic vein; reconstruct the hepatic outflow using an autologous or prosthetic graft (e.g., cryopreserved iliac vein or PTFE) if necessary.  
   • Aim for R0 margins (>1 mm) and preserve at least two contiguous liver segments with intact inflow/outflow.  
- After hepatic recovery (≈6–8 weeks) and completion of adjuvant systemic therapy, perform definitive rectal resection (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal excision) with total mesorectal excision, incorporating any needed pelvic radiotherapy boost.  
- Continue postoperative systemic therapy (e.g., 6 months total) based on response and molecular profile (KRAS/BRAF).  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Exact number of liver metastases and whether they are unilateral or bilateral.  
- Precise extent of IVC/right hepatic vein involvement (percentage encasement, length of contact).  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume and baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve for major hepatectomy and vascular reconstruction.  
- Molecular profile of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide targeted therapy.  
- Any prior systemic therapy already given and the radiologic response to it.

The patient presents with centrally located liver metastases (3–5 cm) in contact with the IVC and the right hepatic vein in the setting of an upper rectal T3N1 tumor, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although the number of lesions is not specified as excessive, the venous involvement makes a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection unsafe without complex vascular control or reconstruction. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only after tumor downsizing and expert HPB / vascular reassessment.

A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvis MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (580 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and reduction of venous contact.

• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the IVC and right hepatic vein.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Multidisciplinary evaluation with complex surgery to assess feasibility of venous reconstruction if required or right hepatomy including en-bloc resection of the right hepatic vein according to the future liver remnant.

• If regression occurs or venous reconstruction is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection with the aim of R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible IVC and/or hepatic vein reconstruction.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

• Given the T3N1 rectal cancer, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning 
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvis MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

F. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic and targeted therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information

   Regimen: oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX or FOLFOXIRI) combined with anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab) – appropriate for NRAS‑mutated disease (anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective).

- Clinical trial consideration  
   Enrolment in a conversion‑therapy trial (e.g., intensified triplet chemotherapy with bevacizumab) or a study evaluating peri‑operative hepatic arterial infusion could be offered, given the high tumour burden and aggressive biology.

- ECOG performance status / Charlson comorbidity index.

Case_Content:
Man, 70 years old, left colon tumor, three liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 200 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. MRI: invasion of the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Superior vascular involvement, significant technical risk, volume to be assessed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The MRI shows invasion of the hepatic‑vein confluence, indicating major outflow involvement that makes an R0 resection technically demanding. The MDT notes “significant technical risk, volume to be assessed.” A decisive piece of information – the future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve – is missing. Without confirmed adequate FLR (≥30 % of total liver volume or >0.5 % of body weight) and a plan for hepatic‑vein reconstruction or alternative hypertrophy strategies, surgery cannot be performed immediately. Therefore the case meets the definition of “Potentially resectable” because a prerequisite (FLR assessment and possible portal‑vein embolization or staged approach) must be completed before definitive surgery.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate conversion systemic therapy:  
   – Preferred regimen for RAS‑wild‑type disease is intensive chemotherapy (FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) to maximize tumor shrinkage and test disease biology.  
   – Treat for 2–3 months (≈8 cycles) with radiologic reassessment after every 2 months.  

• Restaging after neoadjuvant therapy:  
   – Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and CT‑based volumetry to quantify FLR and re‑evaluate hepatic‑vein involvement.  
   – Assess response of all liver lesions (RECIST and morphologic criteria) and confirm absence of new extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum) with chest CT or PET‑CT.  

• Decision algorithm based on restaging:  
   – If FLR ≥30 % (or ≥0.5 % body weight) and hepatic‑vein involvement can be resected with reconstruction (or can be sacrificed with adequate outflow from remaining segments), proceed to curative‑intent liver resection aiming for R0 margins.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal‑vein embolization (PVE) to induce hypertrophy; re‑image 3–4 weeks later.  
   – If hepatic‑vein reconstruction is not feasible or disease remains borderline, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS to achieve adequate FLR while preserving outflow.  

• Timing of primary colon tumor resection:  
   – In a fit 70‑year‑old with left‑sided colon cancer, simultaneous colon and liver resection can be performed if the planned liver operation is limited (e.g., segmental or left hepatectomy).  
   – Given the anticipated complex vascular liver surgery, a staged approach is safer: first perform colon resection (laparoscopic or open) followed by recovery, then proceed with liver surgery after systemic therapy and FLR optimization.  

• Post‑operative management:  
   – Pathology‑driven adjuvant chemotherapy (continue the same regimen or switch to maintenance anti‑EGFR therapy) for at least 3 months.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Precise segmental location, size, and relationship of each metastasis to hepatic veins and portal branches.  
• Quantitative liver volumetry (total liver volume, FLR volume) and functional assessment (ICG clearance, liver biochemistry).  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky), comorbidities, cardiopulmonary reserve.  
• Staging of the primary tumor (T‑stage, N‑stage, presence of perforation or obstruction).  
• Evidence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants) on chest CT or PET‑CT.  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR) and any prior liver disease (steatosis, fibrosis).  

These data are essential to finalize resectability, choose the optimal surgical extent, and tailor the peri‑operative plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, right T3N1M1 colon cancer, four liver metastases (3-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 780 ng/mL, non-V600E BRAF mutation (D594G).
MDT Discussion: Atypical BRAF mutation, intermediate prognosis, bilobar liver involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning  
- Four liver metastases measuring 3‑5 cm each, distributed bilobar, meet technical criteria for resection only if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved (≥30 % of total liver volume in a normal liver). The current case description does not provide FLR volumetry or liver function data, so this key technical prerequisite is missing.  
- The disease is synchronous, CEA is markedly elevated (780 ng/mL) and the tumour harbours a non‑V600E BRAF D594G mutation, both unfavorable biologic factors that traditionally lead teams to obtain a “proof of time” with neoadjuvant systemic therapy before committing to major hepatic surgery.  
- Consequently, resection cannot be performed immediately; it requires (a) assessment of FLR and possibly portal vein embolisation or a two‑stage hepatectomy, and (b) a short course of systemic chemotherapy to evaluate tumour biology and achieve potential downsizing.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy (step‑by‑step)  
1. Baseline work‑up  
   - Obtain full laboratory panel (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, albumin), calculate Child‑Pugh and ALBI scores.  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with liver‑specific contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT) to delineate segmental location of each metastasis and to allow volumetric analysis of FLR.  
   - Record performance status (ECOG), comorbidity index (ASA/Charlson), and confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease (CT chest, PET‑CT if indicated).  
2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate an intensive chemotherapy regimen: FOLFOXIRI (5‑FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan) combined with bevacizumab.  
   - Rationale: triplet chemotherapy provides the highest response rates in BRAF‑mutated mCRC; anti‑VEGF is appropriate because anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective in BRAF‑mutated tumours.  
   - Plan for 3–4 cycles (≈2–3 months), then reassess with imaging and CEA.  
3. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat liver MRI/CT to evaluate tumour response, size reduction, and to recalculate FLR.  
   - If FLR remains <30 % but sufficient hypertrophy is anticipated, schedule portal vein embolisation (PVE) of the liver segments to be resected, followed by a 2‑3‑week interval for hypertrophy.  
   - If disease shows progression or new extra‑hepatic sites, consider alternative strategies (e.g., conversion to systemic‑only therapy, enrolment in a clinical trial, or palliative approach).  
4. Surgical plan  
   - Liver‑first (or staged) approach is preferred given bilobar disease and the need for FLR optimisation.  
   - After adequate FLR is confirmed (≥30 % in a normal liver, ≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected), perform a curative‑intent hepatectomy aiming for R0 margins; this may be a single extended resection or a two‑stage procedure (e.g., right hepatectomy first, then left‑sided resections after hypertrophy).  
   - Simultaneously or subsequently (within 4–6 weeks) perform right hemicolectomy for the primary tumour, unless the primary is symptomatic and requires earlier resection.  
5. Adjuvant therapy  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for a total of 6 months post‑operatively, continuing bevacizumab if tolerated.  
   - Consider enrollment in a trial of BRAF‑targeted therapy (e.g., BRAF/MEK inhibitors) in the adjuvant setting, acknowledging that data for non‑V600E mutations are limited.  
6. Surveillance  
   - CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of chest and abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually up to 5 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- ECOG performance status and detailed comorbidity assessment (ASA/Charlson).  
- Baseline liver function tests and calculation of Child‑Pugh/ALBI scores.  
- Precise volumetric measurement of the future liver remnant.  
- Exact segmental distribution of each hepatic metastasis (to plan resection strategy).  
- Confirmation of KRAS wild‑type status (to rule out co‑mutation).  
- Microsatellite instability / dMMR status (relevant for potential immunotherapy).  
- Explicit statement that there are no extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, nodes).  

These data are essential to finalize the resectability decision and to tailor the peri‑operative plan.

Man, 65 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (2-4 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 320 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. Positive circulating tumor cells detected.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating tumor cells despite no visible extension, prognostic value discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Six liver metastases (2‑4 cm) are not an absolute technical contraindication; resectability depends on ability to achieve R0 resection while preserving ≥30 % future liver remnant (FLR) and adequate inflow/outflow.  
- The case lacks essential information on (a) segmental distribution of the lesions relative to major vessels and biliary structures, (b) quantitative FLR assessment (volumetry, ICG clearance), and (c) functional hepatic reserve.  
- Because the disease is synchronous, high CEA (320 ng/mL) and circulating tumor cells suggest aggressive biology, current guidelines recommend a trial of systemic therapy (“proof of time”) before committing to major liver surgery. Hence resection cannot be performed upfront and must await response assessment and detailed volumetric planning.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Start 6 cycles (≈12 weeks) of a doublet or triplet regimen appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type disease, e.g., FOLFOXIRI + cetuximab (or panitumumab) to maximize response and assess tumor biology.  
   - Monitor CEA and circulating tumor cells after each cycle; obtain restaging contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) at 8–12 weeks.  

2. Re‑assessment of hepatic disease  
   - Determine radiologic response (RECIST) and calculate FLR using volumetric software.  
   - If disease is stable or responding and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ICG‑R15 ≤ 14 %), proceed to curative‑intent surgery.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) of the future remnant lobe, or a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clear lesions in one hemi‑liver, allow hypertrophy, second stage: resect remaining disease).  

3. Surgical sequence  
   - Primary tumor: Perform a left‑sided colectomy (segmental resection or extended left hemicolectomy) either before or concurrently with liver surgery, depending on intra‑operative logistics and patient fitness.  
   - Liver:  
     • If all lesions can be cleared with a single anatomical resection preserving ≥2 contiguous segments and adequate FLR → single‑stage major hepatectomy (e.g., right hepatectomy with wedge resections).  
     • If not, execute the chosen staged approach (PVE → resection or two‑stage hepatectomy).  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance; consider adjunctive thermal ablation or SBRT for lesions in locations unsafe for resection.  

4. Post‑operative management  
   - Pathology‑driven adjuvant chemotherapy (additional 3–6 months) tailored to nodal status (T4N2) and any residual high‑risk features.  
   - Continue surveillance with CEA, imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months, and periodic circulating tumor cell assessment.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Exact segmental location of each liver metastasis and proximity to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
- Quantitative liver volumetry (total liver volume, FLR volume) and functional liver reserve (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT, platelet count).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve), and baseline pulmonary function tests.  
- Detailed staging of extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT, pelvis MRI/CT) to confirm absence of distant metastases.  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (symptomatic vs. asymptomatic, obstruction, perforation) and whether it has been resected or is pending resection.  
- Planned chemotherapy regimen, number of cycles intended, and response criteria to be used.
